clue.text: Unitarian school disciplined statesman

indicators.note: disciplined means knocked into shape, so these letters are drilled into a new order

explanation.surface: A Unitarian school has trained up a politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'statesman' looks like a politician, but here it is playfully a man from a US state.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of a US state can whimsically be called a statesman; this one hails from Columbia's state.

clue.text: Courtesan in play treated with affection

parts.note: to strum is to play a guitar casually
to pet is to stroke fondly

explanation.surface: A courtesan in a stage play is treated tenderly.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are old terms for a woman who sells sexual favours, a prostitute.

clue.text: See 12
Set about working in mine — hurry!

indicators.note: about signals that the word Set is turned around into another order
in places the working piece inside the mine piece

parts.note: a pit is a coal mine
ON means functioning, as a machine is on

explanation.surface: An instruction to a miner to get going on the job, quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is the anagram signal on Set, and 'in' is a container signal; 'mine' is a coal pit, not the possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal imperative urging speed, like 'get a move on'.

clue.text: Pull young lady? Get right in!

indicators.note: in tells us the right piece goes inside the young lady piece

parts.note: a wench is an old word for a girl

explanation.surface: Someone trying to pick up a girl is urged to get stuck in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pull' is British slang for attracting someone, which suits the surface; here it means a hard tug.
explanation.definitionFit: A wrench is a sudden violent twist or tug, a sharp pull.

clue.text: Undoing of woman last month involving the opposite sex

parts.note: Ann is a woman's name

indicators.note: involving means wrapping around, so the last month piece encloses the sex piece

parts.note: ULT, for ultimo, means of last month in old business letters
from the woman's viewpoint the opposite sex is men

explanation.surface: A woman's downfall last month came through dealings with men.
explanation.walkthrough: ULT (ultimo) is old commercial shorthand for last month; 'involving' puts MEN inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An annulment cancels a marriage, undoing it as if it never happened.

clue.text: Legendary flier's the reason fantasy writer gets mentioned

indicators.note: gets mentioned means spoken aloud, so the clue goes by sound

parts.note: the reason is why, as in asking the cause; Jules Verne wrote fantastical adventures

explanation.surface: A mythical flying creature is the reason a fantasy author earns a mention.
explanation.definitionFit: A wyvern is a two-legged winged dragon of heraldry and legend.

clue.text: Detective story — read end!

parts.note: a study is a DEN; putting A DEN inside RED, scarlet, spells out the two clue words

explanation.surface: Someone urged to skip to the last page of a whodunit.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: 'A study in scarlet' as wordplay means A DEN placed in RED, which reads R(EADEN)D.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the first Sherlock Holmes novel, by Arthur Conan Doyle.

clue.text: Clobber dealer senseless following acrimonious face-off

parts.note: knocked senseless is knocked out
F is the abbreviation for following, as in pages ff

indicators.note: face-off removes the front letter of the word

parts.note: acrimonious means bitter

explanation.surface: Someone knocked out after a bitter confrontation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clobber' is British slang for clothes, not a verb here; 'face-off' takes the first letter from BITTER.
explanation.definitionFit: An outfitter sells clothing, which slang calls clobber.

clue.text: Poet's sound recording

indicators.note: recording suggests something heard played back, so we go by how it is spoken

parts.note: a sound is a noise

explanation.surface: A poet's audio recording.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Noyes was an English poet of the early twentieth century.

clue.text: Mate sheepishly, with hurt expression, getting caught — perfect!

indicators.note: getting caught means being trapped inside, so the cry sits within the mating word

parts.note: to tup is what a ram does to mate with a ewe
ouch is what you say when hurt

explanation.surface: An awkward romantic encounter with a yelp of pain and getting caught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mate sheepishly' suggests embarrassment but means mate like a sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: To touch up a painting or photo is to improve and polish it, perfecting it.

clue.text: Upstarts originally in costly house in our avenue — outrageous!

indicators.note: outrageous means wild, so the letters are thrown into new order
originally points to the opening letters of the words in, costly and house

explanation.surface: Social climbers move into a pricey house on our street, to the neighbours' horror.
explanation.walkthrough: 'originally' takes ICH from 'in costly house'; 'outrageous' mixes these with OURAVENUE.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes people newly wealthy and pushing into higher society, social upstarts.

clue.text: Busy day — lawyer's going ape

parts.note: busy is old slang for a police officer, a cop

indicators.note: going means leaving, so the lawyer letters drop out of the day word

parts.note: a DA is a US district attorney

explanation.surface: A hectic day at work sends a lawyer crazy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Busy' looks like an adjective but is British slang for a detective.
explanation.definitionFit: To ape someone is to mimic them, to imitate their behaviour.

clue.text: Where royal profile is exactly right

definitions.meaning: the monarch's head is printed on coins and notes

explanation.definitionFit: Literally on currency, where the sovereign's head appears; idiomatically, accurate.

clue.text: Has to keep English in very poor game

indicators.note: in places the Has piece inside the very poor word

parts.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, of very poor quality

indicators.note: to keep means to hold inside, so Has encloses the English letter

explanation.surface: Someone forced to hang on to English in a dire game.
explanation.walkthrough: PANTS is British slang for dreadful; HEAS (Has holding E) goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Pheasants are game birds shot for sport and food.

clue.text: Damaged the cart's wheel? Maybe

indicators.note: damaged means broken up, so the letters get knocked into another order

explanation.surface: Is the cart's wheel broken?
explanation.definitionFit: A ratchet can be a toothed wheel held by a pawl, one example of a wheel.

clue.text: Monkey, one protected by higher species?

indicators.note: protected by means surrounded, so the higher species wraps the one piece

parts.note: humans are thought of as the higher species
an means one

explanation.surface: A monkey sheltered by mankind, the supposedly superior species.
explanation.definitionFit: Hanuman is the Hindu monkey god, and also the name of the langur monkey.

clue.text: Is linked by time? That's extremely premature

parts.note: something that is linked has ties

explanation.surface: Questioning whether a link with time is premature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is linked' must be rephrased as HAS TIES.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of hasty: done too soon to the greatest degree.

clue.text: Dog getting a stomach upset when man's out

indicators.note: out means outside, so the man word sits around the rest

parts.note: a man is a male

indicators.note: upset in a down clue turns the word upside down, reading it backwards

parts.note: tum is a stomach

explanation.surface: A dog with an upset tummy once its master has left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' reverses TUM to MUT; 'man's out' means MALE goes outside A MUT.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alaskan malamute is a large sled dog breed.

clue.text: One spotted crossing road asleep, so needing treatment

indicators.note: crossing means stretched across, so the scrambled letters span the road abbreviation
needing treatment means in poor shape, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: Someone who dozed off while crossing a road and got hurt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needing treatment' rearranges ASLEEPSO to LEOPAESS; 'crossing' puts RD inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A female leopard has a spotted coat, so it is one spotted.

clue.text: Killer, some say with previous, was falsely arrested

indicators.note: arrested means held, so the previous word holds the scrambled letters

parts.note: old means former, previous

indicators.note: falsely means wrongly, so these letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: A killer, or so it is claimed, was wrongly arrested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some say' nods to doubts over whether Lee Harvey Oswald acted alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Lee Harvey Oswald is widely held to have assassinated President Kennedy.

clue.text: About to cut the old man's hair

indicators.note: to cut means to slice into, so the about piece goes inside

parts.note: the old man is slang for father, so his means dad's
RE means about, concerning

explanation.surface: About to give Dad a haircut.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreads, short for dreadlocks, are a hairstyle of matted ropes.

clue.text: Recalled nice landlady serving Guinness?

indicators.note: Recalled says the hidden letters are read backwards
serving means supplying, so the two words serve up the letters inside them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Remembering a friendly pub landlady pulling pints of stout.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft put 'serving' in the definition, leaving the hidden step with no signal; 'serving' is that signal. Guinness is the actor Sir Alec Guinness, not the stout.
explanation.definitionFit: Alec was the first name of the actor Guinness, star of Star Wars and Ealing comedies.

clue.text: Queen involved in dishonest behaviour? Get outta here!

indicators.note: involved in means placed inside, so the Queen letter goes into the scheme

parts.note: a scam is a swindle
R, for Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: A queen caught up in a scandal is told to clear off.
explanation.definitionFit: An imperative telling someone to go away quickly.

clue.text: Deny making tour of women's prison earlier

indicators.note: making a tour of means going round, so the deny word circles the women letter

parts.note: to negate is to deny
W is the abbreviation for women

explanation.surface: Refusing to take a tour of a women's jail.
explanation.walkthrough: NEWGATE was a notorious London prison, demolished in 1904, hence 'earlier'.
explanation.definitionFit: Newgate was a historic prison in London, long since closed.

clue.text: New entrant soft on crime

indicators.note: soft means pliable, so the letters are moulded into a fresh shape

explanation.surface: A newcomer is lenient toward criminals.
explanation.definitionFit: An incomer is a person newly arrived in a place, a newcomer.

clue.text: Set aside vote? That's not British

indicators.note: not says the British letter is absent from the vote word

parts.note: a ballot is a vote

explanation.surface: Setting aside a vote because it isn't British.
explanation.definitionFit: To allot is to assign or earmark something for a purpose.

clue.text: Strip by Dutch male isn't fantastic

indicators.note: fantastic means fanciful, so these letters are wildly rearranged

explanation.surface: A striptease by a Dutchman that isn't great.
explanation.definitionFit: To dismantle is to take apart, stripping a machine down.
